extracted.intended_audience: seminarians, Catholic theologians, scholars of dogmatic theology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and systematic defense of Catholic doctrines concerning the gratuity and universality of actual (supernatural) grace, including distinctions of merit, types of prayer, capacities, and interpretations of scholastic axioms. Aimed at instructing students and defenders of doctrine in classical theological argumentation and patristic/scriptural proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — prayer for grace and capacity/disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: To pray means to incite God’s liberality or mercy by humble supplication; capacity or disposition (capacitas/dispositio) is a real mode by which a subject becomes apt to receive a new form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes the acts: prayer is an incitement to God’s mercy; capacity/preparation is the subject’s aptitude. Capacity may be positive (entails a claim to the form) or negative (removal of obstacles). Both concepts are necessary to understand the gratuity of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction — congruous merit vs prayer
rubrics_metrics.description: Congruous merit (meritum de congruo) and prayer are distinct because one can exist without the other; angels can pray without earning a merit de congruo, and salutary works can be meritorious without prayer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humble supplication does not involve positive service entitled to a reward. Use this distinction to avoid conflating praying with earning or qualifying for reward in a juridical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction — natural prayer vs supernatural prayer
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely natural prayer (preces naturae) differs from supernatural prayer inspired by grace (oratio supernaturalis); efficacious prayer in matters of salvation requires prevenient grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural and patristic proofs (Rom. VIII; 1 Cor. XII; John XV) show we cannot pray efficaciously without the Holy Ghost. The Second Council of Orange rejects the idea that natural prayer can obtain grace as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive capacity/disposition (capacitas s. dispositio positiva)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive capacity is 'that real mode by which a subject, in itself indifferent, becomes apt to receive a new form.' Such disposition entails at most an expectation based on teleology, not a strict legal claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive capacity differs from quasi-merit: quasi-merit claims fairness-based reward, whereas capacity is preparedness for reception; rewards can be given to others, but introduction of a new form presupposes a disposed subject (e.g., hunger disposed to receive food).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative capacity/disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative capacity consists in the absence or removal of obstacles impeding reception of a new form (e.g., drying green wood to fit for burning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative preparation does not create a strict claim to grace but is relevant to the scholastic axiom that God does not deny grace to one who does what is in him by not opposing grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'gratuity of grace' (gratia prima vocans)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute gratuity refers to the very first or initial grace (gratia prima) by which salvation is begun; this initial grace is absolutely incapable of being merited, and subsequent graces up to justification are also gratuitous insofar as they are based on the prima gratia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Orange and Council of Trent formulations (e.g., grace given without any merits on their parts) are cited; keep separate the idea of merits of grace (rooted in grace) from natural claims to justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis I — nature cannot merit initial grace de condigno
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere nature cannot, in strict justice (de condigno), merit initial grace (gratia prima), nor consequently any subsequent graces in the order of justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is treated as an article of faith; historical errors (Pelagius) and council definitions (Second Council of Orange; Council of Trent) are used as proof. Scriptural proofs (Romans, Ephesians) and Augustinian patristic authority are marshaled against natural merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis II — no natural work creates equitable claim to grace
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no naturally good work by which unaided nature could acquire even so much as an equitable (congruous) claim to supernatural grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second Council of Orange denies preceding natural merits; rebuttals of Semipelagian positions are provided. Scriptural, patristic and theological arguments (grace is cause of merits, so cannot be merited) are presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis III — natural prayer cannot merit supernatural grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature cannot merit supernatural grace even by natural prayer (preces naturae); efficacious prayer is itself an effect of prevenient grace and cannot, unaided, obligate God to bestow grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish intrinsic possibility from divine decree: God could hear natural prayer but is not bound to do so. Scriptural (Rom. VIII; 1 Cor. XII; John XV) and conciliar (Second Council of Orange) authorities are cited; critiques of Ripalda's hypothetical account are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis IV — positive disposition cannot move God to bestow grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Man cannot move God to the bestowal of supernatural grace by any positive disposition or preparation on his part; to suppose otherwise is Semipelagian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: (a) would make grace non-free; (b) patristic teaching and original sin undermine claim; (c) resembles condemned propositions if asserted as a right. Use caution with Molina/contingent-contract theories which attempt to secure grace via natural effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis V — negative preparation can dispose one to receive grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Man may prepare himself negatively for the reception of supernatural grace by not placing obstacles in its way (facienti quod est in se Deus non denegat gratiam understood as negative disposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority theological opinion (sententia communior) holds this; the scholastic axiom admits three interpretations: (a) with aid of grace, God gives further grace (uncontroversial), (b) natural effort per se obliging God (Semipelagian, rejected by many), (c) negative disposition (absence of obstacles) compatible with gratuity. Theological nuance: negative disposition is actual, not causal, and does not make grace owed as justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholastic axiom — 'Facienti quod est in se Deus non denegat gratiam' (interpretations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiom may mean (a) to him who does what he can with the help of grace God grants further grace; (b) to him who does what he can by natural strength God does not refuse grace (Semipelagian reading); (c) to him who does what he can by negative disposition (not placing obstacles) God does not deny grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues for interpretation (c) as orthodox and compatible with gratuity; cites Suarez, Lessius, and historical debates. Warns against interpreting the axiom as establishing a fixed law of distribution of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction — voluntas antecedens vs voluntas consequens (divine will to save)
rubrics_metrics.description: God’s will to save (voluntas Dei salvifica) can be regarded as antecedent (voluntas prima/merciful desire conditional on human cooperation) or consequent (voluntas secunda/just will giving due reward or punishment; connected to predestination and reprobation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to reconcile the gratuity and universality of grace with instances of reprobation; theological analyses (e.g., Augustine, Thomas) and analogies (just judge) are used to show compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3 Thesis I — God wills salvation of all the faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: God sincerely wills the salvation not only of the predestined but of all the faithful without exception; this is treated as an article of faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tridentine anathematizes denial; scriptural proofs (Matthew, John) and patristic testimony support that God earnestly desires salvation for believers. Distinguish at least all the faithful from the predestined in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3 Thesis II — God wills to save every human being (universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: God wills to save every human being; the divine voluntas salvifica is universal, grounded in Scripture (Wisdom XI; 1 Tim. II) and the universality of the Redemption (one mediator Christ Jesus who died for all).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: God’s omnipotence/mercy, mediatorship of Christ (human nature common to all men), and patristic consensus. The thesis is called fidei proxima saltem by the author and is defended against Calvinist/Jansenist objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3 Thesis III — problem of unbaptized infants and universality
rubrics_metrics.description: The fate of unbaptized infants, though a theological difficulty, does not contradict the universality of God’s saving will; the Church has not defined a dogma on their fate and theologians differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: Baptism is ordinary means of salvation; parental/ministerial negligence in administering Baptism cannot be ascribed to Providence; exceptional cases like baptism of blood may save infants. Use caution in drawing universal negative conclusions from this practical difficulty.
